course.title: Social Psychology
course.description: Social psychology studies how the real, imagined, or implied presence of other people shapes what we think, feel, and do. This course surveys its central findings, from attitudes and persuasion through conformity, obedience, group behavior, attribution, prejudice, helping, attraction, and the self. The structure is adapted from the social psychology overview on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), with all explanations written fresh for learners.

questions.prompt: Social psychology is best described as the study of...
options: how brain cells transmit electrical signals
how the real or imagined presence of others shapes thought, feeling, and behavior
the clinical treatment of mental illness
questions.explanation: The field focuses on the social situation and its influence on the individual - see 'What social psychology studies'.

questions.prompt: In persuasion research, the central route to attitude change depends mainly on...
options: the strength and quality of the arguments
questions.explanation: The central route engages careful thought about argument quality; the peripheral route leans on surface cues.

questions.prompt: In Asch's line-judgment studies, many participants gave an obviously wrong answer because...
options: they could not see the lines clearly
the group around them had all given that same wrong answer
they were paid to report falsely
the comparison lines were equal in length
questions.explanation: Group pressure produced public conformity even on an easy perceptual task.

questions.prompt: Milgram's obedience experiments are best known for showing that...
options: people almost never follow harmful orders
ordinary people may obey an authority figure even when told to harm a stranger
questions.explanation: A large share of participants continued delivering what they believed were dangerous shocks when an experimenter insisted.

questions.prompt: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to...
options: blame the situation for other people's behavior
overweight personality and underweight the situation when explaining others' behavior
questions.explanation: We over-attribute others' actions to disposition and underplay the circumstances they faced.

questions.prompt: The bystander effect predicts that a person in trouble is often less likely to get help when...
options: the witness is a trained nurse
the event happens in broad daylight
questions.explanation: Responsibility feels diffused across the crowd, so each witness waits for someone else to act.

questions.prompt: Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort a person feels when...
options: two friends disagree in front of them
they hold conflicting beliefs or act against a belief they hold
a task turns out to be boring
questions.explanation: Festinger described the tension between beliefs and actions that pushes people to change one of them.

questions.prompt: Groupthink describes a decision-making group that...
options: suppresses dissent to preserve harmony and reaches a poor decision
always arrives at the best possible choice
questions.explanation: The drive for consensus crowds out realistic appraisal of alternatives.

lessons.title: What social psychology studies
lessons.grammar_note: Keep the person and the situation as two separate explanations; most behavior is a product of both, and good analysis names each one.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what social psychology investigates, tell it apart from sociology and clinical psychology, and describe how controlled experiments test social questions. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which phrase best defines the field - the study of how the presence of others shapes thought, feeling, and behavior? By the end of this reading you should be able to name the two forces that every later lesson balances, the person and the situation, and say why researchers prefer controlled studies to intuition when they want to know what actually causes a social behavior. You will also be ready to spot the moment when a tidy story about someone's character quietly ignores the circumstances they were placed in, which is the single most useful habit this whole course tries to build.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Social psychology is the scientific study of how the real, imagined, or implied presence of other people influences an individual's thoughts, feelings, and actions. It sits between psychology, which centers on the single mind, and sociology, which centers on groups and institutions; social psychology keeps the individual in view while taking the social world seriously as a cause. Its signature claim is that situations shape behavior far more than untrained observers expect. To test such claims, researchers favor the experiment: they manipulate one factor, hold others steady, and randomly assign participants to conditions so that any difference in the outcome can be traced to the manipulation rather than to who ended up where. Random assignment is what turns a vivid anecdote into evidence about cause. Researchers also define their terms operationally, meaning they decide in advance exactly how 'helping' or 'aggression' will be measured, and they prize replication, since a finding that cannot be reproduced is treated with caution rather than trust.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Gordon Allport gave the discipline its most quoted definition, framing it as the attempt to understand how one person's inner life is shaped by others who are present in fact or only in mind. Kurt Lewin, often called a founder of modern social psychology, captured the whole project in a compact formula: behavior is a function of the person and their environment, written B = f(P, E). Lewin pushed the field toward rigorous experiments and toward what he called action research, the idea that studying a social problem and trying to improve it can go together. Later waves added cognition, asking how people perceive and interpret social information, and the discipline's reference overviews, including the social psychology article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia, still organize the field around that pairing of the thinking person and the pressing situation. Keep these two names handy: Allport for the definition, Lewin for the method and the person-plus-environment formula.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In Lewin's formula B = f(P, E), what do P and E stand for? 2) Why does random assignment matter when a researcher wants to claim a cause? 3) Name one thing that distinguishes social psychology from sociology. 4) What does it mean to define a behavior operationally? 5) Why do researchers care about replication? Answers: 1) P is the person and E is the environment or situation; behavior depends on both. 2) It spreads pre-existing differences evenly across conditions, so any outcome gap reflects the manipulated factor rather than who the participants already were. 3) Social psychology keeps the individual at the center while studying social influence, whereas sociology studies groups and institutions as its primary unit. 4) It means stating in advance the exact, measurable way a concept will be observed, such as counting the seconds before a bystander acts. 5) A result that holds up when the study is run again is more trustworthy than a single striking finding that no one can reproduce.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reducing every social behavior to personality, as if the situation played no part; this course will show again and again that circumstances carry surprising weight. Mistake: treating a single dramatic study as settled proof, when the field trusts patterns that replicate rather than lone headlines. Mistake: confusing correlation with cause and forgetting that only the experiment, with its manipulation and random assignment, licenses a causal claim. Exit: (a) Complete Lewin's formula: behavior is a function of what two things? (b) What research design, above all others, lets a social psychologist say that one factor caused a change in behavior? Answers: the person and the environment (situation); the controlled experiment with random assignment to conditions.

lessons.title: Attitudes, persuasion, and cognitive dissonance
lessons.grammar_note: An attitude is an evaluation (favorable or unfavorable) of something; do not confuse it with a belief, which is simply what a person holds to be true.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define an attitude, describe the two routes by which persuasion changes attitudes, and explain how cognitive dissonance can push a person to change an attitude after the fact. Warm-up: think of an advertisement that won you over with strong reasons and another that won you over with a likable face or a catchy tune; you have just felt the difference between the two routes to persuasion. By the end you should be able to predict when careful arguments will matter most and when surface cues will carry the day, and you should be able to explain the counter-intuitive finding that paying someone very little to say something they do not believe can make them believe it more. These ideas sit at the practical heart of advertising, health campaigns, and everyday debate.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An attitude is a favorable or unfavorable evaluation of a person, object, or idea. Attitudes guide behavior, but loosely: what we do also depends on habits, norms, and the situation. Persuasion research, organized by the elaboration likelihood model, distinguishes two routes. On the central route, a listener who is motivated and able thinks carefully about the content, so argument quality decides the outcome and any resulting change tends to last. On the peripheral route, a listener who is distracted or uninterested leans on surface cues such as the speaker's attractiveness, apparent expertise, or the sheer number of arguments, and any change tends to fade. Cognitive dissonance, introduced by Leon Festinger, works in the other direction: instead of attitudes shaping behavior, behavior reshapes attitudes. When people act in a way that clashes with their beliefs and cannot easily explain the act away, the resulting discomfort pressures them to adjust the belief so it fits what they did.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Leon Festinger is the central name here. In a famous 1959 study he ran with James Carlsmith, participants did a dull task and were then paid either one dollar or twenty dollars to tell the next person it had been enjoyable. Those paid only one dollar later rated the task as more fun than those paid twenty. The twenty-dollar group had an easy external justification for lying, so they felt little tension; the one-dollar group had no such excuse, so they eased the discomfort by deciding the task really had been pleasant. Richard Petty and John Cacioppo developed the elaboration likelihood model that organizes the central and peripheral routes. Carl Hovland and colleagues at Yale pioneered the earlier systematic study of who says what to whom, cataloging how source, message, and audience each affect persuasion. Together these works explain both how outside messages move us and how our own actions quietly move us.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which route to persuasion relies on argument quality, and which on surface cues? 2) In the Festinger and Carlsmith study, which group later liked the dull task more, and why? 3) Give one everyday situation where the peripheral route is likely to dominate. 4) How is an attitude different from a belief? 5) Name one reason an attitude might fail to predict behavior. Answers: 1) The central route relies on argument quality; the peripheral route relies on cues such as attractiveness or expertise. 2) The one-dollar group liked it more, because they lacked a strong external reason for lying and reduced the dissonance by changing their attitude. 3) Scrolling past ads while tired or distracted, when a friendly image can sway you more than any claim. 4) An attitude is an evaluation (good or bad), while a belief is a judgment about what is true. 5) Strong situational pressure, habit, or social norms can override the attitude in the moment.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming attitudes always predict behavior, when the link is real but loose and easily overridden by the situation. Mistake: reading the dissonance result backwards and expecting the better-paid liars to believe the lie more; the opposite is true, because a large payment supplies a ready excuse that keeps tension low. Mistake: treating the peripheral route as mere manipulation; it simply describes how people decide when they are not thinking hard, which is much of the time. Exit: (a) On which route does argument quality decide the outcome? (b) In the one-dollar versus twenty-dollar study, which payment produced the bigger attitude change, and what drove it? Answers: the central route; one dollar, because the absence of an external justification left dissonance to be resolved by changing the attitude.

lessons.title: Conformity, obedience, and the power of the situation
lessons.grammar_note: Conformity is yielding to a group's example; obedience is complying with a direct order from an authority. Keep the two words distinct.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish conformity from obedience, summarize the classic studies by Asch and Milgram, and describe what the Stanford prison study is usually claimed to show along with the serious reasons to read it cautiously. Warm-up: recall a time you went along with a group even though you privately disagreed; was that because you doubted your own judgment, or because you did not want to stand out? Both reasons show up in the research. By the end you should be able to explain why situations can pull decent people toward actions they would never predict of themselves, and, just as important, why some of the most dramatic demonstrations of that claim are weaker as evidence than their fame suggests. Holding both of those ideas at once is the mark of a careful reader of this topic.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Conformity is changing behavior or opinion to match a group. It has two engines: informational influence, where we assume the group knows something we do not, and normative influence, where we go along to be accepted and avoid standing out. Solomon Asch isolated normative influence with a simple perceptual task - matching the length of a line - on which the correct answer was obvious, yet many people echoed a unanimous majority's wrong answer at least once. Obedience is different: it is compliance with a direct order from a perceived authority. Stanley Milgram studied it by instructing participants to deliver what they believed were escalating electric shocks to another person; a striking proportion continued to the highest level when an experimenter calmly insisted they go on. The broad lesson, the power of the situation, is that ordinary people can be led into troubling behavior by the social forces around them rather than by any personal defect.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Solomon Asch designed the line-judgment conformity experiments of the 1950s, showing that even an unambiguous fact can bend under group pressure, while also finding that a single dissenting ally sharply reduced conformity. Stanley Milgram ran his obedience studies at Yale in the 1960s and varied the setup many times, learning that obedience dropped when the authority was less present or the victim more immediate. Philip Zimbardo's 1971 Stanford prison study assigned students to be guards or prisoners and is often cited as proof that roles alone can corrupt. Modern re-examination, drawing on released recordings and participant accounts, has challenged it hard: guards were coached toward harshness, the sample was small and unreplicated, and it was a demonstration rather than a controlled experiment. Treat Zimbardo's study as a vivid hypothesis about roles, not settled proof, and lean on Asch and Milgram, which have been replicated in varied forms, for firmer ground.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the difference between informational and normative influence? 2) In Asch's study, what single change sharply cut conformity? 3) In Milgram's variations, name one factor that reduced obedience. 4) What does the phrase 'the power of the situation' mean? 5) Give one reason the Stanford prison study should be read with caution. Answers: 1) Informational influence is conforming because you think the group is right; normative influence is conforming to be accepted. 2) The presence of even one dissenting ally who gave the correct answer. 3) Moving the authority farther away, giving orders by phone, or bringing the learner physically closer all lowered obedience. 4) The idea that circumstances, not just character, powerfully steer behavior. 5) It was an uncontrolled demonstration with a small, unreplicated sample, and guards were encouraged toward cruelty rather than acting spontaneously.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using conformity and obedience as synonyms; conformity answers group example, obedience answers a direct command. Mistake: concluding from Milgram that most people are secretly cruel, when the studies instead show how situational pressure overrides private conscience, and when obedience fell sharply under other arrangements. Mistake: citing the Stanford prison study as hard proof; its design flaws and coaching make it a cautionary tale about method as much as about human nature. Exit: (a) Which classic study isolated normative social influence on an easy perceptual task? (b) Name one reason researchers now treat the Stanford prison study cautiously. Answers: Asch's line-judgment experiment; it was an uncontrolled, unreplicated demonstration whose guards were coached toward harsh behavior.

lessons.title: Group behavior: facilitation, groupthink, and deindividuation
lessons.grammar_note: Social facilitation is about the mere presence of others changing performance; groupthink is about a group's decision process. Do not blend the two.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how the presence of others changes individual performance, how cohesive groups can reach bad decisions, and how anonymity in a crowd can loosen normal restraints. Warm-up: have you ever performed better in front of an audience on something you knew well, but worse on something you had just started learning? That everyday split is exactly what social facilitation predicts. By the end you should be able to tell social facilitation from groupthink from deindividuation, name the conditions that make each more likely, and suggest a concrete way to guard a group's decision against the pull toward false agreement. These are among the most practical ideas in the course for anyone who works, plays, or decides alongside other people, which is to say everyone.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Social facilitation is the finding that the mere presence of others improves performance on easy, well-learned tasks but hurts it on hard or novel ones, because an audience raises arousal, which strengthens whatever response is dominant. A related effect, social loafing, is the tendency to put in less effort on a shared task when individual contributions are not identifiable. Groupthink, named by Irving Janis, is a failure of decision making in which a cohesive group's desire for harmony and consensus suppresses dissent, discourages outside information, and produces poorly examined choices. Deindividuation describes how people in a large, anonymous group can lose their usual sense of individual responsibility and act in ways they normally would not, whether that means a cheering crowd or a destructive mob. In each case the group does not simply add up individuals; it changes how each person thinks and behaves.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Norman Triplett's 1898 study of cyclists riding faster alongside others is often cited as the first social psychology experiment and an early hint of social facilitation; Robert Zajonc later explained the pattern through arousal and the dominant response. Bibb Latane and colleagues documented social loafing, measuring how effort per person drops as group size grows. Irving Janis built the concept of groupthink from case studies of flawed policy decisions, listing warning signs such as the illusion of unanimity, pressure on doubters, and self-appointed mindguards who shield the group from inconvenient facts; his proposed remedies include inviting dissent, assigning someone to argue the opposing case, and bringing in outside views. Work on deindividuation, developed by Leon Festinger, Philip Zimbardo, and later Ed Diener, traces how anonymity and reduced self-awareness weaken ordinary self-restraint in crowds.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) On which kind of task does an audience tend to improve performance? 2) What is social loafing, and what reduces it? 3) Name two warning signs of groupthink. 4) What two conditions tend to produce deindividuation? 5) Suggest one practical way to protect a group decision from groupthink. Answers: 1) On easy, well-learned tasks, where the dominant response is the correct one. 2) Reduced effort on a shared task when individual input is not identifiable; making each person's contribution visible and accountable reduces it. 3) Any two of: an illusion of unanimity, direct pressure on doubters, self-censorship, or mindguards who filter out dissenting information. 4) Anonymity within a large group and lowered self-awareness. 5) Appoint a devil's advocate, actively invite dissent, or seek input from knowledgeable outsiders before deciding.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming an audience always helps; it helps on easy tasks and hurts on hard ones, because arousal amplifies the dominant response. Mistake: treating groupthink as any group disagreement, when it is the opposite problem of too much agreement too fast. Mistake: thinking deindividuation excuses behavior; it describes a loosening of restraint, not a license, and understanding it is a reason to design for accountability. Exit: (a) Social facilitation predicts worse performance on what kind of task when others watch? (b) Name one of Janis's recommended cures for groupthink. Answers: hard, novel, or poorly learned tasks; inviting dissent, assigning a devil's advocate, or consulting outside experts.

lessons.title: Attribution, the self, and the fundamental attribution error
lessons.grammar_note: A dispositional attribution blames the person; a situational attribution blames the circumstances. Naming which one you are making keeps your reasoning honest.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how people infer the causes of behavior, name the most common bias in those inferences, and describe how the self colors our judgments of our own actions. Warm-up: the last time a driver cut you off, did you think 'what a reckless person' or 'they must be rushing to an emergency'? Your first instinct reveals a bias this lesson is about. By the end you should be able to define dispositional and situational attributions, state the fundamental attribution error and the actor-observer asymmetry, and explain the self-serving bias that lets us claim our successes while blaming our failures on circumstance. Attribution is the quiet engine beneath blame, praise, and much of everyday conflict, so seeing its biases clearly is one of the most useful skills in social psychology.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Attribution is the process of explaining why people, including ourselves, behave as they do. We generally sort causes into two bins: dispositional causes inside the person, such as personality, and situational causes in the circumstances. The fundamental attribution error is the robust tendency, when judging others, to overweight disposition and underweight the situation, so we call a stranger rude rather than stressed. A twist called the actor-observer asymmetry notes that we flip the pattern for ourselves: our own missteps feel caused by the situation, while others' missteps feel caused by their character. For outcomes specifically, a self-serving bias leads us to attribute our successes to our ability and our failures to bad luck or unfair conditions, which protects self-esteem. The self is not a neutral observer; it tilts our explanations in flattering directions, which is why fair judgment of others requires deliberately asking what situation they were in.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Fritz Heider laid the groundwork, describing ordinary people as naive scientists who reason about causes, and his distinction between personal and situational causes underlies all later work. Harold Kelley formalized how we decide between them with his covariation model, which weighs consistency, distinctiveness, and consensus across situations and people. Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error and, with colleagues, demonstrated it in studies where observers credited behavior to disposition even when they knew the situation had forced it. Edward Jones and Richard Nisbett articulated the actor-observer asymmetry. On the self, research by figures including Shelley Taylor and Jonathan Brown explored how positive illusions and self-serving attributions help maintain well-being, and Hazel Markus and Shinobu Kitayama showed that how much weight people give disposition versus situation varies across cultures, with some traditions attending more readily to context.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the difference between a dispositional and a situational attribution? 2) State the fundamental attribution error in one sentence. 3) How does the actor-observer asymmetry change the pattern when we explain our own behavior? 4) What is the self-serving bias? 5) Name one thing Kelley's covariation model uses to decide on a cause. Answers: 1) A dispositional attribution locates the cause in the person's traits; a situational attribution locates it in the circumstances. 2) When explaining others, we overestimate personality and underestimate the situation. 3) For our own actions, especially failures, we lean toward situational causes rather than disposition. 4) The tendency to credit our successes to ourselves and blame our failures on outside factors. 5) Consistency, distinctiveness, or consensus - how the behavior covaries across time, targets, and people.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming the fundamental attribution error means we are always too harsh; it specifically means we underweight the situation when judging others. Mistake: forgetting the actor-observer flip, which is why the same late arrival feels like bad traffic for us but carelessness in someone else. Mistake: treating the self-serving bias as simple dishonesty; it is a largely automatic tilt that guards self-esteem, and merely knowing about it is the first defense. Exit: (a) When we explain a stranger's behavior, which kind of cause do we tend to overweight? (b) Which bias leads us to take credit for success but blame failure on circumstances? Answers: dispositional (personality) causes; the self-serving bias.

lessons.title: Social relations: prejudice, helping, and attraction
lessons.grammar_note: A stereotype is a belief about a group, prejudice is a feeling toward it, and discrimination is an action against it; keep belief, feeling, and action apart.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Separate stereotyping, prejudice, and discrimination, explain the bystander effect and when help is most likely, and name the main factors that draw people together. Warm-up: imagine someone collapses on a busy street while dozens hurry past; would you be quicker to help there, or on a quiet lane where you are the only person around? Your honest answer previews one of the most important findings in this lesson. By the end you should be able to describe the contact hypothesis for reducing prejudice, trace the steps a bystander must pass through before helping, and list the ingredients of attraction. These three threads - how we divide, how we help, and how we bond - together describe the texture of everyday social life.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Prejudice has three linked parts: a stereotype is a generalized belief about a group, prejudice proper is a negative feeling toward it, and discrimination is unequal treatment based on it. A basic driver is the division of the social world into in-groups and out-groups, which breeds in-group favoritism. Helping has its own logic. The bystander effect, uncovered after a widely discussed 1964 case, shows that people are often less likely to help when many others are present, because responsibility feels diffused and each witness looks to the inaction of others as a cue that nothing is wrong. Latane and Darley mapped helping as a series of steps: notice the event, interpret it as an emergency, assume personal responsibility, decide how to help, and act - failing any step stops the help. Attraction, meanwhile, grows from proximity, physical appearance, similarity, and the simple fact that we like those who like us.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Gordon Allport, in his 1954 book on the nature of prejudice, proposed the contact hypothesis: contact between groups reduces prejudice when it meets conditions such as equal status, shared goals, cooperation, and support from authorities. Muzafer Sherif's Robbers Cave study showed hostile boys' groups reconciled once they had to cooperate toward superordinate goals. Bibb Latane and John Darley ran the foundational bystander experiments, including the smoke-filled-room and seizure studies, and formulated both the diffusion of responsibility and the five-step helping model; their work followed public attention to the Kitty Genovese case. On attraction, Robert Zajonc demonstrated the mere-exposure effect, that familiarity breeds liking, while Elaine Hatfield and others studied physical attractiveness and the matching pattern in relationships. Across these works, the practical message is that both hostility and helpfulness respond strongly to how a situation is arranged.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Distinguish a stereotype, prejudice, and discrimination. 2) Why are people often less likely to help in a crowd? 3) List any three of Latane and Darley's five steps to helping. 4) Name two conditions that make intergroup contact reduce prejudice. 5) Give two factors that increase attraction. Answers: 1) A stereotype is a belief about a group, prejudice is a negative feeling toward it, and discrimination is unequal action against it. 2) Responsibility is diffused across many witnesses, and each reads the others' inaction as a sign no help is needed. 3) Any three of: notice the event, interpret it as an emergency, take personal responsibility, decide how to help, and act. 4) Any two of: equal status, common goals, cooperation, and support from authority or law. 5) Any two of: proximity, physical attractiveness, similarity, and reciprocal liking (plus mere exposure).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using stereotype, prejudice, and discrimination as one word; they are belief, feeling, and action, and separating them makes problems easier to target. Mistake: thinking any contact between groups reduces prejudice, when it helps only under Allport's conditions and can worsen tension otherwise. Mistake: reading the bystander effect as proof that crowds are heartless; it is about diffused responsibility and ambiguous cues, and simply naming one specific person to act often breaks the spell. Exit: (a) In a crowd, what process makes each witness less likely to help? (b) Name one condition Allport said intergroup contact needs to reduce prejudice. Answers: diffusion of responsibility (with pluralistic ignorance from others' inaction); equal status, shared goals, cooperation, or support from authorities.
